title: The turning
hookLine: the Mevlevi order's turning ceremony, one hand up, one hand down

cards: The picture travels far beyond Turkey, on posters, postcards and screens: men in tall honey-colored felt hats and long white skirts, turning, turning, skirts flaring out like bells, heads tilted, eyes half closed.
People call them whirling dervishes. It looks like a dance. The people who do it call it something else, and their word is about the ears, not the feet.

teach.b: The word is sama'. It means listening, from the same root as as-Sami', the All-Hearing, one of the names of God. For Sufis, sama' means listening to music, poetry or the Qur'an with the heart until you're moved by it.
The Mevlevi order, named for Rumi, Mawlana, turned that listening into a ceremony.
Tradition says Rumi himself would sometimes turn in ecstasy, and people tell a story that it began when he heard goldbeaters hammering in the Konya bazaar.
The formal ceremony was shaped after his death, by his son and later generations. Everything in it carries meaning. The tall hat is said to stand for the tombstone of the ego.
The white skirt, the shroud. The black cloak they take off at the start, the grave left behind. The music: the ney, the reed flute, and a drum.

teach.h: RIGHT HAND UP, LEFT HAND DOWN.
teach.b: And the arms: right palm up to the sky, left palm down to the earth. As the Mevlevis explain it, what comes from God is received through the right hand and passed on to the world through the left.
The turner keeps nothing. Receive, give. They turn around their own hearts, and they turn together, like planets.
In modern Turkey the orders were closed, and for decades the ceremony survived mostly as a cultural performance. UNESCO now lists it as part of humanity's cultural heritage.
And Muslims hold different views on music in worship: some scholars allow musical sama', and others do not accept it at all.
Those differences come up again soon.

how: Mevlevi Sufis perform the sama' ceremony with the ney and drum, turning with the right palm up and the left palm down; other Muslims, including some scholars, do not use music or dance in worship, and Muslims differ on it.

o: a hymn sung aloud in the mosque at night
a fast kept on Rumi's death day
listening with the heart until it moves you

games.q: you're a turner in the Mevlevi ceremony. one hand receives from God. what does the other hand do?
o: holds on to what was received.
points down, passing it on to the world.
games.why: the left palm faces the earth: what comes from God is passed on. the turner keeps nothing.

practice: If you can stand safely, lift your right hand a little, palm up, let your left hang low, palm down, soften your eyes, and turn slowly once, all the way round, feeling the floor under your feet; then stand still and breathe.
If you can't stand, just turn your palms, one up, one down, and sit with them. Picture receiving through one and giving through the other.

wordCard.voice: Sama'. Listening with the heart; for the Mevlevis, the turning ceremony, one hand up, one hand down. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: listening; in Sufism, listening to music, poetry or the Qur'an with the heart.

carryVoice: Your line: receive, give. One palm to the sky, one to the earth. See you tomorrow.
